content.text: at startup feels like the simplest deployment: every release brings its schema along. Since EF Core 9, a database-wide lock stops several instances from migrating at once, but the bigger risks remain. The running app needs permission to change the schema, old instances keep serving traffic against the new schema, a bad migration takes down every replica as it starts, and nobody reviews the SQL. In production, apply migrations as a separate deployment step.

. The rolling deploy starts the first new pod, which migrates the database and goes healthy. The four old pods are still serving traffic, and from that moment every customer query they run fails with
. Someone hits rollback. The old image comes back, the renamed column doesn't, and the errors continue until a person writes and runs a reverse migration by hand.

when the app starts is the right way to apply EF Core migrations in production. The schema always matches the code that's running, the pipeline needs no extra step, and a fresh environment sets itself up.

There's a lot of truth in it, which is why it spreads. It's the snippet in countless templates, and Microsoft's own docs show it. The biggest classic objection, two replicas migrating at the same time, has been handled since EF Core 9, and the docs now say runtime migration can be acceptable for apps that prefer simple deployment and can tolerate its trade-offs. For a hobby project, an internal tool or an integration test, it's genuinely fine. Production web apps are where the remaining trade-offs bite.
The lock fixed the race, not the rollout

take a database-wide lock before applying anything. In a test with EF Core 10 on SQL Server LocalDB, two processes started together on a database one migration behind. Both logged "Acquiring an exclusive lock for migration application". One applied the migration; the other waited about 5 seconds for it to finish, then logged "No migrations were applied. The database is already up to date."

That's real protection, and it also shows the cost: every new instance is stuck at startup for as long as the slowest migration runs, before it ever listens for requests. A migration that rebuilds a large index holds the whole rollout, and a platform that restarts slow-starting containers can kill the instance that's doing the migrating. On SQLite the lock is a table, and the docs warn it can be left behind if the process dies.
Old code meets the new schema

A rolling deploy runs old and new versions side by side by design. With startup migration, the schema changes the moment the first new instance starts, while every old instance still expects the old one. In the test, a context still mapped to
as soon as the rename was applied. Rolling the app back doesn't roll the schema back, so the old version keeps failing.
The way out is to make every migration compatible with the code that's already running, a technique known as
and copy the data in one release, switch the code to the new column in the next, and drop
only when nothing reads it. Microsoft's guidance for replacing columns follows the same order: populate the new column before dropping the old one.
The app holds the keys to the schema

Applying a migration means creating, altering and dropping tables. If the app migrates itself, the identity it uses for every request needs those permissions too. The docs recommend a separate deployment identity with schema rights, and an app identity limited to reading and writing data. Any bug, injection or compromised dependency in the running app then can't drop a table.
Failures happen at the worst moment
At startup, a failure doesn't stop a deploy; it stops your app. Since EF Core 9,
throws when the model has changes that no migration captures. In the test, one forgotten migration turned into an

before the app served a single request, and every replica would have crashed the same way. And the SQL runs without anyone having read it, though the docs warn that a generated migration can drop a column when you meant to rename it.
The fix: migrate once, before the rollout

# CI: build the bundle from the same commit as the app image
dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes
dotnet ef migrations bundle --self-contained --target-runtime linux-x64 \
  --output artifacts/efbundle

# Deploy: run it once, as a job, with the schema-owner connection
ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production \
  ./artifacts/efbundle --connection "$MIGRATIONS_CONNECTION"
# Then roll out the app, which connects as a read/write-only user

blocks.title: Rolling back the app doesn't roll back the schema

content.text: Whatever applies your migrations, a release whose migration breaks the previous version can't be undone by redeploying the old image. Treat renames, drops and new required columns as multi-release changes, so that the version before and the version after both work on every schema in between.

content.text: Apply the bundle as a one-shot job before the rollout, with a connection that can change the schema. Give the app a user that can only read and write data.
Add columns before using them and drop them a release after nothing reads them, so a rollback of the app never meets a schema it can't use.

items.text: at startup runs on every replica, with the app's own permissions, in the middle of a rollout.
EF Core 9 and later serialize concurrent migrations with a lock, but every new instance waits for the migration before it serves traffic.
Rolling deploys run old code on the new schema, and rolling back the app doesn't roll back the schema.
Apply migrations once per deploy with a bundle or a reviewed script, using a separate schema-owning identity.
Write migrations in expand-and-contract steps so the previous release keeps working.
